metaDescription: Pellet smokers compared by controller type, hopper size, cooking area and portability, from a tabletop model to a 1,539 sq in family cooker.
expertTake: The Z Grills ZPG 550B2 is the pellet smoker to buy if you want a PID controller without a premium badge, and the Pit Boss 500 FB2 is the sensible value pick. Anyone who wants intense smoke flavor on a brisket should skip pellets and look at a charcoal offset.
introParagraphs: A pellet smoker feeds compressed hardwood pellets into a small fire pot with an auger, and a controller adjusts that feed to hold your chosen temperature. It is the closest thing to a set-and-forget wood-fired cooker, and it is why this style has taken over backyards.

The differences between models come from the controller, the hopper, the body and the lid seal rather than from the pellets themselves. A good pellet smoker holds tight temperatures through a windy night, and a poor one chases its own tail.

products.name: Z GRILLS ZPG 550B2 Pellet Smoker with PID Controller
products.description:
The ZPG 550B2 is the one here with the controller most worth paying attention to. A PID controller measures temperature and adjusts both pellet feed and airflow in real time, which holds a set point tighter than the simple timed feed cycles used on cheaper pellet cookers.

Z Grills also builds in a hopper clean-out and a pellet view window, which sound minor but matter in ownership. You can empty the hopper to swap flavors or drain damp pellets, and you can check pellet levels before a long cook. Its 8-in-1 versatility claim covers smoking, grilling, roasting and baking, though a pellet cooker will not match a charcoal grill's sear.

In year three, the igniter and the fan are the parts to expect to replace. Keep the cover on, empty the grease tray, and vacuum the ash from the fire pot every couple of cooks. It is the value pick when you want better temperature control than the Pit Boss 500 FB2 offers but are not looking for WiFi. Its biggest practical advantage over a timed-feed cooker is how it behaves on a cold, gusty evening, when the controller can open the airflow instead of letting the fire sag.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want PID temperature control at a sensible cost.
pros: PID controller adjusts feed and airflow together
Hopper clean-out makes pellet swaps simple
View window lets you check levels mid-cook
cons: Not a sear machine like a charcoal grill
Igniter and fan are wear parts over time

products.name: Pit Boss 500 FB2 Pellet Grill and Smoker, 518 sq in
products.description:
The Pit Boss 500 FB2 combines a wide 180 to 500 F range with a flame broiler lever that exposes direct fire for searing up to 1,000 F. That is rare in a pellet cooker and makes it a genuine two-in-one machine.

The controller moves in 5 F increments and runs on LCD readouts. It is a timed feed controller rather than PID, so it holds its setting less tightly than the Z Grills when wind or cold hits. The 518 sq in cooking area is comfortable for a family of four, or two pork butts.

Treat it like any pellet smoker: store pellets dry, clean the fire pot regularly and keep it covered. It is easy to find parts for, and the smoke quality is respectable rather than outstanding, so it suits cooks who value flexibility over flavor perfection. One habit worth learning early is to preheat with the lid closed for a full ten minutes, because the first temperature reading after startup lags the true chamber heat.
products.bestFor: Families who want a smoker that can also sear steaks.
pros: Flame broiler lever sears up to 1,000 F
Wide 180 to 500 F range for any recipe
Good size for a family of four
cons: Timed feed holds temperature less tightly than PID

products.name: Traeger Pro 22 Pellet Grill and Smoker, 572 sq in
products.description:
The Pro 22 is the entry model from the brand that popularized pellet smokers. Its main advantage is a mature ecosystem: parts, accessories and replacement pellets are everywhere, and the design is well understood.

It offers 572 sq in of cooking area, more than the 518 sq in on the Pit Boss, but caps at 450 F where the Pit Boss reaches 500 F. The 18 lb hopper is generous and suits an overnight cook.

Expect to replace the igniter eventually, and keep the hopper dry. It will not impress anyone with features, but it is a durable, proven cooker with the easiest parts supply in the category. Because it is so widely sold, almost every question you will have has already been answered by a forum post, which is a real advantage for a first-time owner. Use the same dry storage habits as any pellet cooker, and replace the igniter before it fails rather than after a ruined cook.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want a proven design and easy parts supply.
pros: 572 sq in is generous for the size
cons: Few extras compared with newer rivals

products.name: Pit Boss 150 Portable Tabletop Pellet Grill and Smoker, 256 sq in
products.description:
The Pit Boss 150 is a tabletop pellet smoker designed to travel. A latch-locking lid and two handles let you carry it to a campsite or tailgate, and it still reaches the same 180 to 500 F range as its bigger siblings.

With only 256 sq in of area, it is a small-batch machine. Expect to cook a rack of ribs or a handful of chicken pieces, not a full brisket. Compared with the 518 sq in 500 FB2 it has half the space but a fraction of the footprint.

Because it needs a power source, it is only portable where you have a plug or a battery pack. It is a great secondary smoker for travelers, and a reasonable primary one for singles and couples. The small hopper means a lower-temperature cook needs a refill sooner than on the full-size models, so check pellet level before you start and keep a bag nearby. Space is the real constraint: a single rack of ribs needs to be cut in half to fit, and two chickens will crowd the grates. Porcelain-coated grates clean up with a quick brush, and the lid latches shut so grease does not slosh around in the car.
cons: Needs a mains outlet or power source

products.name: Traeger Woodridge Pellet Grill and Smoker, 860 sq in, WiFi

specList.label: Functions
specList.value: Grill, smoke, bake, roast, braise, BBQ

products.description:
The Woodridge scales up the Traeger approach with 860 sq in of cooking area and WiFi control from an app. Its 180 to 500 F range is controlled and monitored remotely, which is genuinely useful on overnight cooks.

The larger body means more steel to heat, so expect longer preheat and more pellet use than the Pro 22. The area is enough for a whole brisket plus a rack of ribs, which the smaller models cannot manage.

Because it relies on a WiFi connection, check signal range from your patio. It is the most capable of the Traeger line here, and the right pick for families that cook for crowds. Grease management matters more on a cooker this size, since more fat drips through a wider grate area, so line the tray and empty it before each long run. The porcelain and steel body is built for weather, but a fitted cover still extends the life of the electronics noticeably. If your patio sits at the edge of the WiFi range, a cheap range extender solves the biggest complaint owners have with app-connected cookers.
products.bestFor: Large families and anyone who wants app control.
pros: 860 sq in handles brisket plus sides
WiFi app lets you monitor remotely
cons: App needs a stable WiFi signal

products.name: Pit Boss 1600 Navigator Pellet Grill and Smoker, 1,539 sq in
products.description:
The 1600 Navigator is the largest pellet smoker here, with 1,539 sq in of listed cooking surface. It includes WiFi and Bluetooth connectivity, a touchscreen controller and the same flame broiler as the smaller Pit Boss models.

At this size you can smoke multiple briskets or cook for a large gathering. The tradeoff is that it takes up a big footprint and burns through pellets faster than any other pick here.

Like all pellet cookers, it needs a nearby outlet and dry pellet storage. It is a serious cooker for large groups, and overkill for a household of two. Preheat is slower at this size, so give it extra time before the meat goes on, and expect pellet use per cook to be noticeably higher than on the 850 Navigator or the 500 FB2. Plan on a level pad and a clear path to roll it, because a unit this large does not fit through narrow gates. If you only ever cook for four, the smaller Pit Boss models will give you the same flavor with less fuel and less cleanup.
cons: Burns more pellets than smaller models

buyingCriteria.explanation: A PID controller like the Z Grills 550B2's measures temperature and adjusts both feed and airflow, so it corrects errors before they grow. A timed-feed controller, like the Pit Boss 500 FB2's, pulses pellets on a fixed schedule and drifts more in wind. For long brisket cooks, PID is worth the premium. For ribs and chicken the difference is minor.

Hopper capacity dictates how long you can run without refilling. The Traeger Pro 22's 18 lb hopper suits an overnight smoke at low temperatures, while smaller hoppers need a top-up mid-cook. Hopper capacity matters more than total area for unattended cooks.

For two to four people, roughly 400 to 500 sq in is sufficient, which is where the Pit Boss 500 FB2 at 518 sq in sits. The Pit Boss 150 at 256 sq in is small, and the Pit Boss 1600 at 1,539 sq in is for crowds. Larger units burn more pellets and take longer to preheat.

Pellet smokers typically top out at 450 to 500 F. The Traeger Pro 22 reaches 450 F, while the Pit Boss and Traeger Woodridge reach 500 F. If you plan to sear, look for a flame broiler like Pit Boss's, which reaches 1,000 F on direct flame.

WiFi, as on the Traeger Woodridge and Pit Boss 1600, lets you watch an overnight cook from bed. It only matters if your signal reaches the patio, and it adds electronics that can fail. A model with good probes and PID control may be more useful than an app.

Pellets absorb moisture and swell, which jams the auger. Store them in a sealed bin, not the hopper, between cooks. A hopper clean-out like the Z Grills 550B2's makes swapping or draining pellets easy.

howWeEvaluated.title: Controller quality
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared PID, timed-feed and app-connected controllers. The Z Grills 550B2's PID ranked first for tight control, while the Pit Boss 500 FB2's timed feed scored well on flexibility.

howWeEvaluated.title: Hopper and capacity
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at hopper size and cooking area together, since both set how long and how much you can cook. The 18 lb Traeger Pro 22 hopper was a benchmark.

howWeEvaluated.title: Temperature range
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared ceilings from 450 F on the Traeger Pro 22 to 500 F on the Pit Boss and Woodridge, and weighed whether a flame broiler adds real searing capability.

howWeEvaluated.title: Portability and footprint
howWeEvaluated.description: The 256 sq in Pit Boss 150 and the 1,539 sq in Pit Boss 1600 sit at opposite extremes. We scored how well each size fits its likely use.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership support
howWeEvaluated.description: Parts availability, wear items like igniters and augers, and cover or storage needs were weighed. Established brands scored higher for long-term support.

rows: Wide range with a flame broiler

cards.label: PID
cards.text: The Z Grills 550B2 adjusts feed and airflow together, which keeps temperatures tighter in wind and cold. It suits long cooks like brisket.

cards.label: Timed feed
cards.text: The Pit Boss 500 FB2 pulses pellets on a fixed schedule. It is simpler and fine for ribs and chicken, but drifts more.

howToChoose.note: Pick PID for brisket and overnight cooks, timed feed for casual use.

howToChoose.subheading: For Brisket and Overnight Cooks Specifically

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A large hopper, tight temperature control and enough area to fit a full packer brisket, with probes that report remotely.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Traeger Woodridge at 860 sq in with WiFi is the best fit, with the Pit Boss 1600 for very large cooks.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You cook for groups, want remote monitoring or plan to run overnight brisket. The Woodridge and 1600 Navigator reward that.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You cook ribs, chicken and sausages for a small household. The Pit Boss 150 or 500 FB2 cover that well.

maintenance.why: Ash chokes airflow and causes flameouts. Check the igniter hole is clear.
Grease can ignite in a hot cook. Replace liners if you use them.
Damp pellets swell and jam the auger. Use a sealed bin.
A greasy probe misreads temperature and confuses the controller. Wipe it gently.
Rain and humidity shorten the life of the hopper, igniter and electronics.

faq.q: Do pellet smokers produce real smoke flavor?
faq.a: Yes, but it is milder than a charcoal or stick-burning offset. Smoke mode and lower temperatures give the strongest flavor.
For long cooks and windy locations, yes. A PID controller adjusts feed and fan together and holds tighter temperatures. For short cooks the difference is small.

faq.q: Can I use a pellet smoker without electricity?
faq.a: No. The auger, fan and igniter all need power. A portable power station can work for a tabletop model like the Pit Boss 150.
Use 100 percent hardwood pellets without fillers. Flavor pellets like hickory, apple and mesquite change taste slightly.

faq.q: How much does a pellet smoker burn?
faq.a: It depends on temperature and weather. Low and slow uses far less than a hot cook, and cold wind increases consumption.

faq.q: Can a pellet grill sear steaks?
faq.a: Models with a flame broiler like Pit Boss can sear on direct flame. Others reach 450 to 500 F, which cooks steak but does not match a charcoal sear.
